title: Vesper and the Clock
premise: In the winter of 1863, Sebastian Sterling works as a battlefield nurse in a river town where the war's official record is being written by men who never held a dying soldier's hand. Keeping a private ledger of the names officers omit—deserters, women in uniform, the enslaved and the forgotten—she believes she can stay invisible until a census taker named Elias Vesper begins asking questions that threaten to expose her ledger, her past as a runaway heiress, and the found family of wounded soldiers and freed workers sheltering at her hospital. As spring thaws approaches and the victors' historians arrive by steamboat to seal the official account, Sebastian must choose between duty to the family who disowned her and love for Elias, whose own orders may require him to erase everything she has built. She races to get the truth on record before the ice breaks, testifying before the historians at great personal cost; the book ends with her ledger entered into the public archive under both her names, her found family intact, and Elias choosing her over his commission.
about_author: Gideon Galloway is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing Civil War hospital records in the Ohio River Valley. Their novels are known for excavating the small, stubborn documents through which ordinary people contradicted official history.

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboard
chapters.summary: Sebastian Sterling, POV. In a converted riverfront hotel serving as a field hospital, Sebastian finishes another twelve-hour shift and adds three omitted names to her hidden ledger. The emotional beat is quiet defiance: history happens elsewhere, she tells herself, while the first snow seals the town in.

chapters.title: A Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Sebastian, POV. Census taker Elias Vesper arrives to count the hospital's residents and lingers on anomalies: a nurse with no marriage record, soldiers listed under wrong regiments. His final question—'And what name were you born under?'—lands like a shellburst. Beat: the past knocking at the door.

chapters.title: The Sterling Name
chapters.summary: Flashback woven into present, Sebastian, POV. We learn she fled a wealthy Cincinnati family rather than marry the man chosen for her, trading silk for aprons and taking a dead brother's name. Present-day: she lies to Elias smoothly, then hates how easily she lied. Beat: shame curdling into resolve.

chapters.title: Ward Four Keeps Its Own Records
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter anchored by Corporal Amos Reed, a Black soldier recovering in Ward Four, POV. He discovers Sebastian's ledger and, instead of reporting it, offers her the names of his company's dead that no officer bothered to record. Beat: the found family forms around a shared act of witness.

chapters.title: Ice on the Ohio
chapters.summary: Elias, POV. Elias files his census report but keeps one page back—a copy of the hospital roster he can't stop studying. His supervisor hints that 'historians from the capital' will arrive before thaw to fix the region's official narrative. Beat: complicity beginning, conscience stirring.

chapters.title: The Surgeon Who Signs Other Men's Work
chapters.summary: Dr. Harlan Pike, POV. Pike takes credit for amputations performed by his overworked subordinates and grows suspicious of Sebastian's nighttime writing. He warns her that unauthorized records constitute sedition under army regulations. Beat: institutional menace made personal.

chapters.title: What the Officers Omit
chapters.summary: Sebastian, POV. A botched engagement upriver floods the wards; Sebastian records a lieutenant's cowardly order to abandon the wounded, names included. She realizes her ledger has stopped being memory-keeping and become evidence. Beat: fear transmuting into purpose.

chapters.title: Tea with the Enemy Historian
chapters.summary: Sebastian, POV. Advance historian Miss Cordelia Ash arrives early, sharp-eyed and sympathetic but bound to the War Department's line. Over tea she praises Sebastian's 'excellent memory' and asks, casually, whether anything here contradicts the official dispatches. Beat: temptation and danger in one voice.

chapters.title: Elias Returns Without His Ledger
chapters.summary: Elias, POV. Ordered to verify discrepancies in his own census, Elias instead burns his duplicate pages and confesses to Sebastian that he falsified the count to protect the hospital. Between them, something unspoken becomes spoken. Beat: love declared against duty, quietly, by lamplight.

chapters.title: The Letter from Cincinnati
chapters.summary: Sebastian, POV. Her father's attorney arrives demanding she sign away her inheritance or be publicly exposed as a deserter of her class. The letter includes a clipping about her 'disgrace.' Beat: the old family tightening its grip just as she finds a new one.

chapters.title: Amos Testifies to No One
chapters.summary: Amos, POV. Amos dictates testimony about the abandoned wounded to Sebastian, knowing no court will hear a Black corporal. He asks only that it exist somewhere. Beat: grief dignified; the ledger's moral weight becomes unbearable and sacred at once.

chapters.title: Pike Finds the Floorboard
chapters.summary: Sebastian, POV. Dr. Pike discovers the hiding place during an inspection; the ledger is seized and locked in his office pending the historians' arrival. Sebastian must decide whether to steal it back. Beat: catastrophe, and the family rallying around her instead of scattering.

chapters.title: The Night Shift Conspiracy
chapters.summary: Ensemble, rotating close-third among nurses, patients, and Elias. They plan the theft for the night of the grand ball Pike hosts for the arriving historians. Each character volunteers for the role most likely to destroy them. Beat: solidarity crystallizing into action.

chapters.title: The Ball at the Hotel Sterling
chapters.summary: Sebastian, POV. In a borrowed gown she moves through Pike's ball, dancing with the lead historian while Elias lifts the ledger from the office above. Cordelia Ash watches them both too closely. Beat: elegance stretched over terror; a kiss exchanged as cover and as truth.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Landing
chapters.summary: Elias, POV. A ward boy sells them out; Pike intercepts Elias at the steamboat landing, and the ledger is recovered—but not before Elias hides the most damning pages inside his official census folio. He is arrested as a accomplice. Beat: sacrifice, and the plan half-saved.

chapters.title: What Duty Requires
chapters.summary: Cordelia Ash, POV. Cordelia interrogates Elias and realizes the truth of the omitted names; she faces her own choice between the department's narrative and the record. She reads Amos's dictated testimony and cannot put it down. Beat: the antagonist's conscience turning the story's key.

chapters.title: Before the Ice Breaks
chapters.summary: Sebastian, POV. With the river groaning and cracking, Sebastian makes her play: she will testify openly, under her real name, surrendering her anonymity to make the ledger admissible. Her father's attorney arrives to stop her; she signs nothing and walks past him to the hearing room. Beat: the cost paid willingly.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Sebastian and Cordelia, alternating POV. Before the historians, Sebastian reads the omitted names aloud; Cordelia, breaking with her department, enters the ledger and Amos's testimony into the official record. Pike's forged reports unravel. Beat: climax—the private truth becoming public history.

chapters.title: Pike's Reckoning
chapters.summary: Pike, POV. Stripped of his command and facing court-martial, Pike confronts Sebastian one last time, insisting he protected the hospital in his way. She answers with the list of men who died of his omissions. Beat: the villain humanized but not forgiven; justice without triumphalism.

chapters.title: The Ice Breaks
chapters.summary: Ensemble, Sebastian anchoring. The river shatters open overnight; the steamboats carrying the sealed official history depart with Cordelia aboard—and with copies of the true record hidden in her trunks. The town breathes. Beat: release after long pressure; winter ending on every level.

chapters.title: Two Names on One Page
chapters.summary: Sebastian, POV. Elias resigns his commission; his superiors accept, relieved to bury the scandal. He and Sebastian marry quietly in Ward Four with the whole household as witnesses. She writes both her names—Sterling and her birth name—in the ledger's front matter. Beat: love against duty resolved into love remaking duty.

chapters.title: Vesper and the Clock
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Sebastian, POV, years later. Now a schoolteacher, she receives a printed volume citing 'the Sterling-Vesper deposition' as a primary source; Amos's testimony appears in full. At dusk she winds the hospital's old clock, kept as a relic, and adds one more name to a new ledger: a student's father, still unrecorded. Beat: inheritance passed forward; witness as a lifelong vocation.
